extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys (practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph — i.e., whether the disclosure teaches one skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Covers factors, burdens of proof, examples, correlation, predictability, and examiner procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference [R-3]
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of repeating some information contained in another document, an application may attempt to incorporate the content of another document or part thereof by reference in the specification. The information incorporated is as much a part of the application as filed as if the text was repeated in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing the identified material incorporated by reference with the actual text is not new matter. See 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p) for Office policy regarding incorporation by reference. See MPEP § 2181 for the impact of incorporation by reference on the determination of compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph when 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Enablement Requirement [R-2]
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention as defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to ensure the invention is communicated to the public in a meaningful way. The requirement does not demand teaching a commercially viable or perfected embodiment absent a claim limitation to that effect. Enablement is separate and distinct from the written description requirement and must be analyzed under its own criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Enablement / Undue Experimentation Standard [R-5]
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is tested by whether one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure and the knowledge in the art without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard derived from Mineral Separation v. Hyde and In re Wands. The question is whether necessary experimentation to practice the invention would be undue or unreasonable; some experimentation may be acceptable if not undue. A patent need not teach what is well known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (A): The breadth of the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth of the claims is a key factor in determining whether the disclosure enables the full claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide claim breadth may require more detailed disclosure; enablement must be commensurate with claim scope. See MPEP § 2164.08 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (B): The nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of the invention (e.g., chemical, mechanical, biotech) affects the enablement analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature of invention influences how much detail is needed; nascent or unpredictable technologies generally require more specific teaching. See MPEP § 2164.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (C): The state of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: What one skilled in the art would have known at the filing date informs the amount of disclosure necessary for enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A richer prior art may reduce the amount of disclosure required; the state of the art is evaluated as of the filing date and cannot generally be supplemented by post‑filing publications except in limited circumstances. See MPEP § 2164.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (D): The level of one of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The skill level of the person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) determines what must be taught in the specification for enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the pertinent art in terms of the problem to be solved. The higher the skill, the less explicit detail may be required. See MPEP § 2164.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (E): The level of predictability in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictability of the art (ability to extrapolate results) affects how much experimental guidance is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less predictable arts (e.g., many chemical and physiological areas) demand more detailed disclosure; in highly predictable arts a single embodiment may suffice to enable a genus. See MPEP § 2164.03 and examples cited (In re Marzocchi, In re Fisher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (F): The amount of direction provided by the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: How much guidance, instruction, or procedural detail the specification supplies to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The greater the direction and guidance in the specification, the less likely experimentation will be considered undue. Examiner should evaluate the nature and sufficiency of the direction provided. See In re Wands discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (G): The existence of working examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification includes working (actual) examples or prophetic examples, and how those examples relate to the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working examples are persuasive, particularly in unpredictable arts, but are not required. Absence of working examples is a factor to consider but never alone dispositive. See MPEP § 2164.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (H): The quantity of experimentation needed based on the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of trial-and-error or screening necessary to make or use the invention given the disclosure and knowledge in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the required experimentation is extensive such that it would be undue, the disclosure may be non-enabling. Examiner must weigh quantity together with other factors (In re Wands). See MPEP § 2164.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Make the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose at least one method for making and using the claimed invention that bears a reasonable correlation to the entire scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose alternative methods does not automatically invalidate a claim. If practice requires special starting materials or apparatus not readily available, the application must provide sufficient disclosure of them. Transitory intermediates need not be taught in stable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Use the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach how to use the claimed invention, but it need not specify details (e.g., dosage) when standard modes are known to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is limited by a particular use, enablement is evaluated with respect to that use. For compound/composition claims without a recited use, any enabled use that reasonably correlates with the entire claim scope can suffice. If multiple uses are disclosed, an enablement rejection must explain why each disclosed use is not enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Example (working vs. prophetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in a specification may be based on actual work (working) or predicted outcomes (prophetic); the presence or absence of examples is not dispositive for enablement but is a factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant need not reduce the invention to practice before filing. Lack of a working example is considered more strongly in unpredictable arts. A single working example can preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, but may not alone establish enablement across broad claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: None or One Working Example — limits on rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of working examples should not be the sole reason for a non-enablement rejection; conversely, a single working example is often enough to preclude a blanket non-enablement rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of one working example should not automatically be interpreted as enabling the full breadth of claims without analyzing other factors; examiner must explain why extrapolation from the example would or would not be expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation: in vitro / in vivo
rubrics_metrics.description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example constitutes a working example only if it 'correlates' with the disclosed or claimed method of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art recognizes the model as correlating to a condition, accept correlation unless evidence shows otherwise. Examiner bears the initial burden to give reasons for lack of correlation; rigorous or exact correlation is not required (Cross v. Iizuka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Examples and a Claimed Genus
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus claims, representative examples plus a statement applicable to the genus may be sufficient to enable the genus as a whole if one skilled in the art would expect use across the genus without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of enablement may be required for un exemplified members only where the examiner advances adequate reasons to show a person skilled in the art could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of Predictability of the Art and the Enablement Requirement [R-2]
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of guidance needed in the specification is inversely related to what is known in the prior art and the predictability of results in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nascent or unpredictable technology requires specific and useful teaching. In predictable arts (mechanical, electrical) a single embodiment may provide broad enablement; in unpredictable arts (chemistry, physiology) more species/examples are generally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the Examiner Under the Enablement Requirement [R-1]
rubrics_metrics.description: Before rejecting for non-enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and establish a reasonable basis to question enablement, giving specific reasons and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must select and state definitions for ambiguous terms, explain why the disclosure is doubted, and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning (In re Marzocchi, In re Bowen). The first Office action should present the best case with all relevant reasons and evidence, and examiners should identify limitations that would render claims enabled where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of Enablement Based on Evidence as a Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement conclusions are reached by weighing all evidence; once examiner establishes a prima facie basis to question enablement, applicant must present persuasive arguments or evidence to show enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit declarations/affidavits or references; such evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention and consistent with the specification as filed. Examiner must weigh all evidence and not rely on personal opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Must Be Enabling as of the Filing Date [R-2]
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is judged based on what the specification and the state of the art taught as of the application's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-filing publications generally cannot be used to show what was known at filing, though they may sometimes provide evidence of what skilled artisans would have known by that date. The state of the art at filing affects predictability and need for working examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Must Be Enabling to Persons Skilled in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person skilled in the pertinent art (the PHOSITA) to make and use the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pertinent art should be defined relative to the problem to be solved. The level of skill in the art, as of the filing date, determines what needs to be disclosed for enablement.
